title: The divided votes, member by member
question: On each divided roll call where a lobbying client had a stake, who voted the client’s way, who voted against, and which of them had received money from the client’s circle?
finding: 46 divided roll calls are set out in 46 rows (a file with clients on both sides has a row for each): 36 final Board votes, 2 other Board votes on the same measures where a member voted differently, and 8 committee votes. A client’s side can be read for 23 of the final votes, in 23 rows: the client’s side won 22 and lost 1. On those final votes, members who had received money from the client’s circle in the two years before voted the client’s way 25 of 32 times (78.1%); members who had not, 162 of 215 (75.3%); by the test in the screen on votes that difference is within chance. The client’s side lost on 200455 (2020-06-23, 10 to 1). In 20 rows the clients only monitored the measure or asked for changes, so no side can be read.
how: Every roll call with at least one aye and one no is taken from the Board’s vote pages for money files and for measures a lobbyist cited by file number (2015 to November 2026), and from the vote pages for land-use matters. A roll call is listed when it is the Board’s vote on the measure itself or a committee’s vote to send it on, and the file is one of three kinds: a measure that a lobbyist’s contact report cites by its six-digit number, with a contact dated in the three years up to the vote; a contract, lease or other money file whose title names as the other party a client then paying a lobbyist (gifts and grants the City receives are left out); or a land-use matter from the vote test of the two previous screens. What the client asked for is read from the “outcome sought” on the contact: support or approval counts as wanting passage and opposition as wanting defeat; the other party to a money file is taken to want it passed; for an appeal only wording that says which side should win is used. The words in quotation marks are the outcome sought most often, as the lobbyist typed it. “Final Board vote” is the Board’s last roll call on the measure itself; another Board vote on the measure is listed only when a member voted differently on it. Where the vote page lists no member, the votes are those printed in the Clerk’s published minutes of the same meeting, and the link opens the minutes. On the client’s side “won” means the motion carried where the client wanted an aye, or failed where the client wanted a no, as the result is printed on that vote page; the file’s later fate is in the last column. Fees are all payments from those clients to those firms in the calendar years from two years before the vote to the year of the vote, whatever they were for. A dollar figure after a supervisor’s name is what the client, its officers, its lobbyists, their firm and the firm’s staff contributed to that supervisor’s committees in the two years before the vote. Supervisors are named; givers who are not registered lobbyists, firms or clients are inside those sums and are not named. Rows where a side can be read come first, final Board votes before earlier readings and committee votes, the closest votes first.
limits: Lobbying is registered, and so is giving by a lobbyist’s clients and colleagues. An official can sponsor or vote for something a donor wants because the official already favoured it; a donor can give to an official because of what the official already stands for. These 23 final votes are the few divided ones among 307 tested, and the test in the screen on votes finds what is said there; a row here is one vote, not a pattern. Supervisors vote in blocs for reasons of politics and district that have nothing to do with a client, so the members on one side of a roll call are not independent of each other. The positions come from a few words typed by lobbyists and are read by fixed word lists; a measure can be amended between the contact and the vote, so that a client who backed the first version may not back the last, and a business group can “oppose” a measure it later accepts. The other party to a money file is read from its title and matched to a lobbying client by name; it has usually won a department’s competition before the Board votes, and the amount is not always money to the client: in a sale or lease of City property the client pays the City. A member shown as excused may have been out of the room or may have stepped aside; the page does not say which. Ordinances that no lobbyist cited by number are not among the pages on disk. For 332 roll calls the Clerk’s vote page says “by the following vote” and lists no member, 306 of them dated 2016-04-13 to 2016-07-26; 315 were read instead from the vote lines in the Clerk’s published minutes of the same meeting, and 17 remain without member votes and are counted nowhere here. 2 files (160358, 160657) are left out wherever a final vote is counted or tested: for their last passage vote the vote page lists no member and the minutes print the action twice with different tallies, so it is not counted as unanimous and no earlier reading stands in for it. 43 divided votes on amendments, continuances and re-referrals of these files are not listed, because an aye there cannot be read as for or against the client; nor are 4 divided votes on gifts or grants a client made to the City, nor 17 other Board votes, mostly first readings, on which no member voted differently from a later vote on the same file. A private payment for an official act cannot be seen in any of these records, and nothing here says one was made. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
